_note: PRD R11. Prompts only — the client renders these verbatim and stores what the user types. Nothing here is inferred from the transcript and nothing ever should be: a guessed name in an advocate's packet looks like evidence.
intro: Record what you can see now. A buckle number written down at the roadside is worth more than a name remembered next week — and if you can only get one thing, get that.

fields.label: Buckle number
fields.hint: The number on the metal plate or shoulder tag
fields.why: The most reliable way to identify an officer later, and the detail most often missing from a complaint.

fields.label: Name
fields.hint: As given, or as printed on the name tag
fields.why: Useful, but names are common and sometimes given loosely. It supports the buckle number rather than replacing it.

fields.label: Police station
fields.hint: The station they said they are from
fields.why: Decides where a written complaint goes first, and which senior office supervises it.

fields.label: Police vehicle number
fields.hint: Registration on the jeep, van or bike
fields.why: Ties the encounter to a duty roster even when nobody gave a name.

fields.label: Rank
fields.hint: Constable, head constable, sub-inspector, inspector — or the stars if you can only see those
fields.why: Narrows who it was, and some procedures turn on the rank of the officer carrying them out.

fields.label: Unit or wing
fields.hint: Traffic, local police, armed reserve, something written on the vehicle
fields.why: Traffic and local police are supervised by different offices, so this can change where the complaint goes.

fields.label: Anything else you can see
fields.hint: How many of them, what they were wearing, anything distinctive
fields.why: When there is no number and no name, this is what is left. Write it while you can still see them.
